BUSTER SMITH (Interviewed by Stanley Dance):
When did you start to play music?
I started in about 1924.
1924? Not before then?
It might be in '23... The Fall of the year.
Was that the time when you literally first bought an instrument, or when you first started to play professionally...?
Yes.
Were you not messing around with some music as a child?
No, no.
Not at all.
No. I was in the country, and bought on credit. That was in '21.
Was it '22?
Yeah. You bought a clarinet in '22.

Yeah. And then when ...(?)... (?)... out there in the country, and changed the mood in town. We moved here in '23. That white guy who was in the (?). Jones? John(?) Lasiph(?) [PHONETIC] We didn't play nothin' but truck houses. Played blues, nothin' but blues. Truck houses.
When you started out on clarinet, was there anybody that you'd heard on record? Had you listened to any records? Was there anybody you were trying to model yourself on or style yourself on?
Buster Smith - 2
Yes. Uh-huh.
Who was that?
The man I always admired as playing the horn was Sidney Bechet.
You'd heard records of Sidney Bechet.
Yes. But he was playing the soprano sax, and I tried to copy behind him. I'd buy all his records and listen to him. Sidney Bechet.
Because he hadn't made too many records by then.
No.
I think the first records he made were with Armstrong in 1924. And he made some records with Louis Armstrong...
Yes.
There was a thing like "Texas Blues" and "Dallas Blues"...
Yeah, he had one of the choruses. "Kansas City" in some of them...
"Kansas City Blues."
Yeah, "Kansas City Blues." That was the one he played all that horn on. Yes.
Let's consider Sidney Bechet for a moment. By comparison with other people playing saxophone and clarinet at that time, he seems to me to have been very much ahead of everybody else then.
Yeah, he was. Yeah, that's what I think. That's my idea. He was ahead of everybody...that I've heard of.
Buster Smith - 3
Now, in 1922 or '23, or thereabouts...
Yes.
...I believe that you played with a little band from New Orleans.
Yes.
Can you remember anybody who was in that band?

Yes. There was a trumpet player by the name of Don Albert. His real name is Albert Dominique, but he changed his name to Don Albert because later on he organized a big band around here. Yeah, Don Albert.
Did he come to live in this area, then? In Dallas?
Yeah.
He's not still around, is he?
No, he's back in New Orleans now. But he stayed in San Antonio for years and years.
And he's still alive?
Yes. Last I heard of him, last year, he's still alive.
How do you people keep in touch with each other? How do you find out all this?
When he comes to town... He come here this week.
Really..
Yeah, yeah. He used to... Of course, there was a school year. At Booker T. Washington School I have a big friends
Buster Smith - 4

-- Professor Patton. And he hung around with Professor Patton when he'd come to town, and he'd stay two to three days with him. Then they'd together and come out here and visit me. But Professor Patton passed about three years ago, so I haven't seen him since. But he was down there running the (?), something around there called Red something, man, where he had a big club. And Don Albert ran that club for him for years and years down there. They called it Red Something -- I forget its last name.
Now, if you can remember back that far, this little band from New Orleans that you played with...
Yes?
What kind of music was it? Was it what they call gutbucket music? Blues and all that sort of stuff?
Yeah. The Blues! Rhythm-and-blues. Rhythm-and-blues, yes. Particularly rhythm-and-blues.
And again, I can only relate these things to recordings that I've heard of bands at about that time.
Yes.
Was there any band that you were trying to sort of resemble in any kind of way? Who were you models for the kind of music you were playing?
Well, there was two of them. Duke Ellington and Fletcher Henderson.
Those were both bands which used a certain amount of
Buster Smith - 5
arrangements. In other words, were you trying to get these little arrangements together to get that kind of overall sound?
Yeah, that's right.
Even as early as 1924.
Yeah, yeah. Back then, yeah. Heh-heh. Fletcher Henderson... A lot of these ideas were from records that he had then. I learned how to arrange, and how to voice the instruments and whatnot. Yes.
And at this stage, when you would have been only 18 or so, or 20...
Yes.
Were you able to read music at that stage of your life?
No. No, I wasn't reading music.
Was there anybody in the band who did read music?
No. Not that little small band. They didn't bring the music up(?). They just played by ear up there. We had about five pieces together. We played in a place called the Tip-Top.
Yeah, that's the place. That's right. That was in Dallas..
Yeah. Down on the Central.
Were most of the other guys from New Orleans as well?
Yeah. The trombone player and the banjo player and an alto player. I was the only Dallas boy who was in the band. The rest of them was all from New Orleans.
Buster Smith - 6
How did you come to join the band? Why did they pick you?
Well, I was the only one playing clarinet.
They needed a clarinet player?
Yeah, they wanted a clarinet player. See, they had an alto player, and Don Albert was on trumpet. And they had a trombone player and then the banjo player.
Now, one of the big names on clarinet at that time was Johnny Dodds. How did you rate his playing?
Oh, no... Jesse Hooker was the one I....
Jesse Hooker. You had heard him.
Yeah. He was one of the clarinet players around here.
He was a Texas boy, wasn't he.
Yeah. A little short fellow. He was a whole lot of player. He was one of the best ones around here. Jesse Hooker.
What about Jimmie Noone?

Jimmie Noone was all right. I didn't get to meet him. But Jesse Hooker, I hung around... I used to follow him around. I'd go up and listen to his band before we went up there and play behind them, when... They were often working around here and play (?) house in the daylight, and I'd follow him around and listen to him play. So it gave me ideas.
[PAUSE]
Buster Smith - 7
How long was it before you started to play alto? When did you pick up alto?

I picked up alto in '25, it was. Yeah, '25. We got another little band together... No, I was in this three-piece band, the first band, ...(?)...: , a boy named Jesse Dee. He was a drummer, and he had an alto and drums, too. So he didn't like the alto, so he let me have his old alto.
And this would have been when? 1925 or before?
Yes, that's right. It was about '24!
Because there weren't too many alto players around at that time?
No. There wasn't too many around. Let me see... Sauerkraut, he was about the best one around here.
I don't know that name.
They called him Sauerkraut, but his name was M.J. Collins. He's supposed to be in Chicago somewhere. He quit playing several years ago.
The only names I know on alto at around that time are people like Stump Evans, who was a Chicago man.....
Yes.
And there was somebody else...I can't remember who else. But I mean, I don't even know from recordings.
Yes.
And you only know the guys who got recorded. But what I'm
Buster Smith - 8
interested by is that my impression of alto playing in the very early 20's is that it was rather stiff...
Yes.
...and the played it rather like a brass horn.
Yes.
There wasn't much fluency.
No.
Other than Sidney Bechet.
Yes.

Now, where did you get this idea from, to get all over the horn and move very fast on it? Because the funny thing is, I get the impression that your alto playing was much more fluid than your clarinet playing.
Yeah. Well, I used to listen to Tommy Dorsey (ha-ha) quite a bit. Then another cat in there, (?)Woodie Walder(?)...
Yes.
And all of them cats, played all that technique of the instrument. And I had all of their records. So I'd follow behind them, and add a little something to it.
As far as getting technique on the instrument was concerned, would you buy instruction books...
No. Never.
Really?
Buster Smith - 9
Never did.
When you used to practice, did you used to practice scales and all that kind of stuff?
No, no, never did.
You never practiced scales.
Never did. Uh-huh.
So all you would do would be that you would try to get the melody...
Yeah.
And then think of ideas to implement(?).
Yeah.
You never did any of those scales and arpeggios and all that kind of stuff.
No. Never did. When I joined up the big band... The biggest band I joined in them days, the first big band in fact, was the Blue Devils. And they came...
That was in about 1925?
Yeah.
And you were playing only alto with them. Or did you play clarinet?
Yes, I played clarinet and alto. I told them 'I can't read.' 'That's all right. Read the (?) books, and you can start right on the course.'
How did they get to hear about you? Did they hear you play
Buster Smith - 10
someplace?
Yeah.
Or did you go and sit in with them?

No. They came here in the summer, and hung out here. In fact, they got here and got stranded around here. Yeah. They came here with about eight pieces and they got stranded around here, and couldn't get out of town. So they stayed around here about a year-and-a-half or two years, and they geared the band back up. And Ernest Williams came out to my house and got me.
He was just the vocalist, or...?
No, he played drums.
He was the drummer with the band?
Yeah, he was the drummer with the band.
Because at one stage, you had this man, Willie McWashington, didn't you? You had him on drums at some stage, didn't you?
No.
With the Blue Devils?
No. We had this boy right here.
Oh, maybe Willie McWashington was with Bennie Moten.
Yeah. He was with Bennie Moten. Ernest Williams.
[EDWARD McNEIL IS CITED AS THE BLUE DEVILS' DRUMMER IN JAZZ STYLE IN K.C. & THE SOUTHWEST]
That's the drummer we had.
He is not living now.
Buster Smith - 11
Yeah! He's in Kansas City. If you go down there at the Palm Beach Club, you'll find he's down there every day. On (?) and Oakland(?). He's there every day.
Now, let me get this straight. So what had happened was that you'd played clarinet with a little trio of your own, doing the truck houses.
Yes.
Then this New Orleans band had arrived.
Yes.
You joined them, you were with them about a year...?
Yes. About a year.
Was there anything between then and your joining the Blue Devils?
No.
And am I right in thinking that at you joined the Blue Devils in 1926?
Yeah, maybe '26... I think it was '25.

'25. Coleman Lewis(?) and myself, we... He's a clarinet player, too. So they wanted him, too. So we both went with them. We went to Oklahoma City... They went to Oklahoma City, and they were going to make that their headquarters -- that's where they used to stay all the time anyhow. Went up there, and they played the big holiday dates, and they didn't
Buster Smith - 12
give us enough money. They gave all the boys the right salary, and said, '(?) playing with us too.'
They didn't pay you at all.
Yeah. They gave us about ten or fifteen dollars less than they did the other fellows.
Why was that?
I don't know. We quit, went off from the band, left and come back to Dallas.
Then they came back and got you again?
Yeah. They come back next spring... That was in the Fall of the year -- I think it was the Halloween dates that we played. And next spring they come back to Dallas and picked us up again.
And you said 'This time you'll pay us the right money.'
Yeah. We stayed with them then. Stayed with them til they...
Now, I'm very interested in the kind of music that the Blue Devils were playing in 1926. For instance, let's make a simple comparison.
Yeah.
By comparison with the music that you were playing with that New Orleans band, was it similar or different?
Yeah, it was different.
What were the differences?
Buster Smith - 13

Yeah, it was different. It was more Uptown music. More (?)Lucky Hill(?) and Red Allen playing in bands ...(?).... Because those boys from New Orleans, they had a kind of Dixieland, a rhythm-and-blues and Dixieland music. Everybody was mostly for themselves. There wasn't no teamwork.
No section work.
No.
But the Blue Devils had good section work, too?
Yes. They had arrangements to read.
And who was doing those arrangements?
Walter Page wrote a little bit.
He was with the band already then?
Uh-huh. Yeah, oh yeah.
he was playing brass bass?
Yeah.
Not string bass then.
Yeah. He was playing strings, the upright bass.
Even in 1926?
Yes! He had a big upright bass. Let me see... No, he didn't.
He played the tuba.
Yeah, he had a tuba. Yeah, that's what it was.
Okay. So you had arrangements and Walter Page was doing some. Who was playing piano with the band?
Buster Smith - 14
Willie Lewis.
Now, the only Willie Lewis I know is an alto player who went to Europe, but this must be a different one.
No, this here is a different fella. He's from Peoria, Illinois. He was what they call one of those gay fellas, you know. He was a very great musician.
Really.
Yes.
Is he still alive?
No, he's dead. He got burned up in a house. ....[INAUDIBLE SENTENCE].... in Peoria, they tell me.
[PAUSE]
Now, these arrangements... Like you say, more kind of arranged music that the Blue Devils were playing.
Yes.
Was this again the kind of arrangements that you would have heard on recordings of the time by Duke Ellington and Fletcher Henderson? Or was there some difference? Was it a different kind of style?

Yeah, a different kind of style. A little more around the orchestrations. They got these little orchestrations they'd hand out... They'd hand out this little stuff to you. It wasn't too heavy. Every (?) they'd write there's a bit of (?). They didn't write nothin' too stiff where the guys had to
Buster Smith - 15
rehearse on it so long before they could get it down, because they didn't have time, so they could make these dates.
Are you saying that they would buy stocks?
Yes. Oh yeah, they had a whole trunkload.
And these were not being written by anybody in the band. You could buy them.
Yes.
And there would be a part for each instrument.
Uh-huh.
And then they'd just play those?
Yeah.
But as far as getting a sort of particular sound, their own kind of sound to those...
Yes.
How did they do that?

Well, they didn't really... In fact, they didn't start that until I learned how to write for the saxophones. Then I started adding saxophone choruses in there. Regular choruses that one man would be getting off on, it would be three or four was getting off on at the same time in a harmony.
We'll come to that in a minute. Again, I'm very concerned with 1926, the very early days when you were there. Was the band playing a lot of blues material?
Yes.
Buster Smith - 16
Was it blues material like this, or was it blues material more in the style of Ma Rainey and that kind of slow stuff?
Yeah, yeah.
Both.
Ma Rainey... It was both of them.
Really?
Yeah. In fact, we did both of them.
Did you have a singer with the band at that time?
Only Ernest Williams was singing.
I see. Now, I have a question here about Jimmy Rushing. When you joined in 1926, Jimmy Rushing was...?
Yeah, yeah. He was the that was doing all the singing then.
He was in the band.
Yeah.
And not Ernest Williams. Or both?
Yeah, Ernest Williams was there, too. But Williams was playing drums.
So they'd share the vocals.

Yeah. But Jimmy Rushing did mostly all the singing. He left first. I think he left the band first, and then Joe Keyes left and went to Bennie Moten. Then Ernie Williams had to do a little singing that we had.
All right. Can you remember how long Willie Lewis stayed
Buster Smith - 17
with the band? I think Basie joined in '28.
Umm...
Didn't Basie join the band in '28?
Yeah, he did. In 1928.
Why did Willie Lewis leave? What happened?

Oh, he just got tired and went over to... I can't think of that boy... What's that boy's name? Anyway, he just got tired and they kept on after him and he went on there with them, with just that little band, and they hung around up in Arkansas and all around in Tulsa quite a bit. So he just went on over there anyway. There wasn't any misunderstanding or nothing. He just got tired.
When Basie joined, did he join from working with the Whitman Sisters, or was he...?
He wasn't doing anything.
Oh, he wasn't.
No.
There's a theory that maybe he'd been sick and he was recovering from being ill.

Not that I know of. All he did was hung around down on 18th and Lydia Street down in Kansas City, down there in the flat. All around there, there was guys talking about Basie -- William Basie, that was his name. A nice piano and he wasn't doing nothing. So after Willie left, Willie Lewis, then we sent
Buster Smith - 18
and got Basie.
Had you heard him play before?
Yes?
Was he given an audition? Did they say, 'Hey, come on down and sit in with us'?
Yes. Just 'come on down.'
Did you try out anybody else at the same time?
No.
Boy, I guess you were lucky to get him.
Uh-huh. And he wasn't down there that long before Bennie Moten sent down right here...sent for him to come back to Kansas City, and he played with his band.
That would have been '31 or so.
Yeah. So that's why we had to get these other boys. We got Turk... Did we use Turk? Turk Thomas...
Yeah. One question I've got down here... Basie came to Dallas, then, with the band.
Yes.
We sent for him to come down here and join the band here. The band was already here.
Now, the other man I'm very interested in is Hot Lips Page, the trumpet player.
Yes.
Buster Smith - 19
How did he come to join up with the Blue Devils? What happened?
We heard about him down here in Tyler, Texas.
He was from Tyler, wasn't he?

Yeah. That was his home, in Corsicana. But he was in a little band down there called Sugar Lou and Eddie. That's the band he was with. He had a little seven-piece band there. So we heard about it. So we ran into him... We ran into him somewhere. Anyway, he got the wind that we wanted him. So he came to Dallas and joined the band.
He wasn't happy with Sugar Lou and Eddie?

I don't remember. I mean, we had a better band. I guess a better band, and we was working more. I think Sugar Lou and Eddie, they only worked on weekends or something... Well, not only. But we used to play from town to town and every night.
So you were a pretty popular band.
Yeah. We was about the most popular band around, around down in this part of the country in them days.

That clears that up. I'm going to talk a lot about Lester in a minute. But just for the moment, the only question I want to know about is how did Lester come to join the band. Because I think you heard him in Minneapolis or something like that?
Yes.
What happened?
Buster Smith - 20

We went to Minneapolis and played the dates/the bass(?) there, and we got through playing that night, and we went down where Lester was playing with Frank Hine and Eddie Barefield. It was about seven or eight pieces. So we went up there, and they played until I guess two or three or four o'clock in the morning. Anyway, we went up there and had dinner. Then they asked me to sit in with them and play somethin'. So I got in and played three or four numbers. So we...
Now, just a minute. Lester was playing alto then or tenor?
No, he was playing tenor.
Really.

Yes. See, they didn't have but two horns, and Eddie Barefield, he was on alto, and Lester was on tenor. So we stayed all night until late next day, and then we had to go back on the highway. So, "We like that tenor player, we'd like to get him" -- because the tenor player we had, he could just read but he didn't take no solos. And "We'd like to get that cat."
Who was the guy?

Reuben Roddy. He was from Pueblo(?). So we wanted Lester, and sent the boys up to talk with him, and when they went to talk with him, he says, "Oh, I can't leave." So we went away and stayed about a week away. Went back on the highway (and we all bought two or three new cars in the band), and went back to Minneapolis. We drove in front of Lester's house, and he
Buster Smith - 21

sees these new cars, he thought this big band is making a whole lot of sense. We said, "Man, you better come on and go with us. You see what we've got here?" He went up and packed his suitcase, we got him some pinto beans... What's those beans they called? I forget.
Pork and beans?
Pork and beans. Yeah, we got him some pork and beans, put 'em in the suitcase, and come out there...
What did you need them for?
He loved pork and beans.
Really?
Yeah, man.
I have to find out what these beans are.
Yeah, yeah!
Are they like black-eyed peas?
Oh, yeah, yeah. Down in this part, the musicians, you find 90 percent of them, man, they love them pork and beans. Yeah.
But you can't be suggesting to me that you all went out and bought cans just to get Lester in the band.
Yeah! He come in and ...(?)... Then when we were done with it, he stayed with us until we were out of (?) .
How long did it take for him to find out you weren't so rich after all?
Buster Smith - 22

Oh, he just liked the boys. That was a band more brother-like. The guys out there were all good to each other. If a guy got broke and he wanted to borrow some money or they got hungry and needed some money, they'd all chip in and let him have some.
Was that unusual?
Yes, it was.
For a band to be like that?

Yeah, yeah, it sure was. Yeah. Jimmy Rushing was one man that wouldn't lend nobody else a dime. He didn't care how hungry you got and how broke you were and what condition you were in. That's Jimmy Rushing. He wouldn't give you a quarter. But all the rest of the boys, Walter Page, Hot Lips Page, even Bucket -- he was the first bandleader. All them. They gave something. They would all let you have money. If you wanted to borrow some money, if they got any...
Incidentally, Hot Lips and Walter weren't related, were they.
No. They had their names spelled different. Their last names were spelled different.
Oh really? I didn't know that.
Oh yeah. Walter Page was 'Paige.'
He's never spelled that way on record.
Yes. And Hot Lips was 'Page.'
Buster Smith - 23
I didn't know that.
I see his brother down here every week. He only had one brother...
Now, you had a problem with your arrangements being stolen someplace.
Yes. St. Louis.
They were Blue Devils arrangements.
Mmm-hmm. Yes.
So, this wasn't with Basie. This was the Blue Devils.
The Blue Devils, uh-huh.
Who took them?

I'll tell you how that happened. Were we goin' to Virginia or coming back? I think was goin' to Virginia. Let me see. Yeah. On the way going to Virginia, and this boy... We had stayed there two or three days before we could leave to get on our trip, on account of we had ...(?)... on our bus. And this boy had a big house. He says, "You boys, come on up and stay at my house. I won't charge you much. Come on up and stay." And he had a restaurant right next door to his house.
This was in St. Louis.

In St. Louis. So he said, "Just put all your instruments and your music, put it in the bag...put it right here in the restaurant, and he said, "When we get through tonight, we lock up and ain't nobody gonna bother them." When we got ready
Buster Smith - 24

to leave in the next day or so, I didn't pay no attention. I picked the music up in the bag, and ...(?). He just went in the bag and stole the music, (?)half the arrangements(?). We got on to Virginia and found out somebody had been in and stole some of our best arrangements out of there. So I think we had to borrow from a white man who come through there who used to write for Paul Whiteman -- he fixed them up for us.
Really?
Yeah. He stole those.
But what did he need them for? He wasn't a working musician, was he?
Yeah, he had a little old band around there. See, we didn't know it. He was a drummer. I think he was a drummer.
Did you ever see him again?
No. We never did see him no more. See, we left there. We never did come back to his place no more.

I have a friend in London who wanted me to ask you about another musician from Kansas City. I'll come back to the Blue Devils in a minute, but I want to get all his stuff over first. There was this guitar player called Efferge Ware.
Ware...
Do you know the man I mean?
No...
He used to play guitar. He was like a rhythm guitar player.
Buster Smith - 25

No, there wasn't but two guitar players that I knew... No, wait a minute. There's three. There was one called Christmas. He's still living, he's still there. Then Fiddler -- Claude Williams. He's still there. We just played together last year. And there's a boy there called there Jim Daddy, a big fat...
Oh, Walker. Jim Daddy Walker.

Yeah, Jim Daddy Walker. He was the best guitar player around. He was a hell of a guitar player. He died. And then another boy called Cliff. A red, tall boy. He did some arranging. I think he did. He used to play with Georgia Lee. And they were the four guitar players I knew around there.
Incidentally, the tune you're most famous for is "One O'Clock Jump."
Yeah.
Do you still get royalties from that?
I ain't ever got no royalties.
You never got any royalties.
No, I didn't. I didn't even get a time.
That's outrageous!
Yes sir.
How could they do that?
Well, trust the man. You see, I made the number up... It was in the Reno Club with Basie...
Buster Smith - 26
I know the story of how it was made.
Yeah, you know how it was made?
Well, you had to find a signature tune or something, and you were playing... Well, you tell the story, because maybe I don't remember exactly.

Basie always...he's always experimenting on something. You see, I played first also. He always relied on me to add something to it, make something out of it. So he started playing blues in F. You know, we mostly played a whole lot of heads down there in the Reno Club -- we only had about eight pieces down there. So he said, "I want to play a little blues..." He called me Prof. He said, "I want to play a little blues in F here, and then I'm going to D-flat." He said, "You put something to it."
You mean, he was telling you this while he was playing in F?
Right before he started.
Oh, before he started he said, "I'm going to play down a couple of choruses in F, and then I want you come in D-flat."
Yes. "Put something to it, set something to it, add something to it, and make the cats fall in." I said, "I will. You wait until you get to D-flat; I'll set up something."
Did you have an idea at that stage what you wanted to do?
Oh, yeah-yeah-yeah.
You knew what you wanted to do.
Buster Smith - 27

Yeah. All that I wanted to do was just change keys. If he didn't change keys, I would have said something. But put the D-flat so it would sound weird(?), and get that beautiful tone. And I put the alto just right. And the other cats all fall in underneath there, with the harmony and everything. So we played the first night, and everybody, even the boss man, said, "You all play that tune that the band ...(?). . . jumpin' them keys." He said, "You all play that again." We had to play it three or four times a night. I set them saxophone riffs, until I could tell ...(?). . . and you'd tell them where to go to. Whether to put it in there with the ...(?). . . or whatever you wanted to put in there. Hot Lips was playing first trumpet, but we had Joe Keys on first trumpet. Yeah. And the only way the band could get away a lot of times, we had to go out the back door. Step out one at a time. All that kind of stuff.
Oh, wow!
Yeah.
Did it ever happen to you as a band or bands you knew that actually the band would get beaten up or get (?) out of town?

No. Wouldn't hardly none of 'em get beat in (?) because they'd go along with them until they'd get out of town, if you had to hurry and get out of town and all that kind of stuff. You wouldn't get beat up. You had to go along with 'em until you could get away from there.
God, it must have really made you hate them.
No. We just figured that people were just ignorant, just didn't know any better.
Well, that, of course, is a very mature way of looking at
Buster Smith - 56
it.
Yes. Uh-huh.
I'm amazed you were that philosophical, frankly.
Yeah. See, news like that travels fast, you know.
Stay out of that town.
Yeah. Uh-huh.

I remember Milt Hinton telling me about some time when he was with one of these bands (I can't remember which one), and there was like this little room underneath the bandstand. And they got locked in there. And they heard all these guys outside who were talking about setting fire to the building.

Yeah. Well, we never had nothing like that. But we ran into... When we more or less stopped playing and didn't ...(?)..., there'd be some guy who got drunk. While we was in Oddlow, Oklahoma, playing on the second floor for a man who had a dance hall up there, with the White police, in a White place(?) and everything. And the boss man paid us off at 11 o'clock. We had to play til 12. And he paid us off, and then he left. The people were just sitting there ...(?)... We had to play til 12 so the people could get their money's worth. And everybody left, except one great big guy who looked like a big prizefighter. He looked about 32 years old. He pulled off his shirt...he'd got drunk and pulled his shirt off. Got up with nothin' on but his pants, and pulled his shoes off, and he got right at the door
Buster Smith - 57
where we had to come out with all our instruments. He said, 'I'm gonna whup every one of you when you come out, one by one.'
He was going to hit you all.
Yes. He said, 'You all think you're smart. I'm gonna whup every one of you.'
And what happened?

Well, at 12 o'clock I said to ..(?).., 'We don't want no trouble; we've got to get out of here.' Wasn't no police, nothin' around. We looked out the window out there, wasn't nothin' out on the street. No cars, nothin'. All home. The guy says, 'Come on out. I'm gonna whup every one of you when you come out of here. One by one, I'm gonna whup every one of you.' So we got to thinking, said, 'What we going to do.' We didn't want no trouble. ...[INAUDIBLE SENTENCE].... jump on that man and start running. ...[INAUDIBLE]...
This is Reuben Lynch.

Reuben Lynch. Then he said, 'You all want to get out?' We say, 'Yeah, sure. We got to get back to Dallas. We got to go home.' 'Just follow me.' We had some music stands made all out of steel, you know, like these schools use -- old-timey. He just got one of them, folded it up. 'Follow me.' He rolled that thing and batted that guy right in the back of the neck, draw that thing and batted him clean down the steps with that thing, right down into the street. The man said, 'Whoever
Buster Smith - 58
did that, I'll kill you. I'll bust your brains out." But see, we all got in the car and flew! Ha-ha!
There must have been incidents which could have got really nasty. For instance, you're playing White dances. Right?
Uh-huh.
Now, there must have been times where some ignorant White guy would get drunk and accuse one of the musicians of giving the eye to his girlfriend or his wife.
Oh, no! No.
It never happened?
No. We didn't get them (?).
No, I'm sure you weren't doing it.
Yes.
Did they ever accuse you of doing that? Did they ever say, 'Yeah, you were. I saw you...?'
No. Not in the Blue Devils.
You were lucky, because in fact, that's the way a lot of guys got lynched.
Yeah. That's right.
And they didn't do anything!
No, not that... We used to have trouble with the police we'd get in them towns and things like that. They don't want to ...(?). . .(?). . .
How were the police on the whole? Were they there to
Buster Smith - 59

Most of the White dances, there was no police around there. The man, he did everything. In other words, you didn't have no ruckus or nothin' around there. Some of those places... Right down in Oklahoma City, there was a place we used to play there over the weekend called the Forest Park. It was a White place, and it was kind of like a (?). And this man had this dance hall out there, and he'd give a big dance out there on Friday and Saturday. And there was fellow who came here, called him Texas Slim, and he'd get drunk and start a fight with four or five guys in there. And the boss man had to call the police from uptown to come out there and corral him. Because he'd get out there in the yard and jump on everybody.
He was a White guy.
Yeah. A White fellow. But he didn't bother us. No, he didn't bother the band.

Was there much of a feeling among the White people who would go to these dances... Did they feel that the Black music had something that the White music didn't? Did they seem to feel that you were very good at playing?

Yeah, yeah. Not only that, we ran into... There was a dance down here in Palestina... See, we knew how to handle all the (?)s... We still didn't think about that. We watched out for that. And we ...(?). . .(?). . . down there at Palestina.
Buster Smith - 60

We went down there the first time, and we played out on kind of like a lawn(?)... A great big band(?), and they had a big lawn, a big (?) spread out there, and people was dancin' on it. The sheriff comes down with two big pistols on, and he wouldn't let nobody dance but himself! In other words, he didn't want nothing but "Turkey In The Straw" all the time. And we had to play "Turkey In The Straw." So Walter Page, he was leading the band... I told Walter, "There's a man who says he don't want us to play nothin' but 'Turkey in the Straw' all the time for him," and wasn't nobody dancing but him, by himself, standing out there with some big boots on, right in the middle of the floor, and the people are all standing... He's a bad man, so wasn't nobody said nothin' to him; all the people were standing around and listening to it!
How long did that go on for?
It went on the whole night while we played!
You're kidding!

So the boss man said, "He's the baddest man in this part of the country." So he said, "Go ahead, I'm paying you. Go ahead and play. Don't make no difference. There's nobody gonna dance." He said, "I'm gonna pay you anyhow."
Could you actually play "Turkey In The Straw"?
Yeah! Sure, we played it. Sure. We had to play it! We better play it! Ha-ha.
Buster Smith - 61
Where was this?
In Palestina, Texas.
Sort of cowboy country, is it?
Well, the cowboy country mostly was back out in West Texas. But this here was down in Southeast Texas.
Did you used to play out in Western Texas?

Oh yeah. We played all back out there. I used to go out there quite often. When (?) was in the band, we used to go all out there. But things had changed, most(?) in those days. The one time we went down there, and we're sitting up on the bandstand, and the man walked up there and looked... We was up on the second floor this time. And two or three guys come around there. So we took an intermission and they came back, and sort of looked at us. "Where are you boys from?" We told them, most of them, "Oh, we're from Texas. We're from Dallas." See, we knew all that. Some of them boys were from way up in the old North, but they'd tell 'em they was from Texas.
Keep everything cool.

Yeah. Staying cool. So one guy said to ..(?).., "See that big fat nigger laying out there, sitting there?" He was talking about Jimmy Rushing. He said, "My daddy sure could use him down on his plantation." He said, "He got three full niggers down there like him. I sure could use him down there, because he could kill a whole lot of hogs and things." We just
Buster Smith - 62
sat there and looked at him.
You had to keep really cool.

Yeah. We just sat there and looked at him, and after intermission over we started back playing. They didn't bother us no more. See, what they were trying to do was trying to start something. But we knew better.
Do you never remember a case with any other band where really trouble started?

Yeah. I think it was the Blue Aces. They were out near Beaufort, Texas, way out in West Texas. The cowboys came into the place and shot all the lights out at the top of the house, except a few, and the man told band "Don't stop until they say 'Stop.'"
Don't stop playing.

Yeah. Play until they get tired. The only way they got away from that, everybody left one by one. See, they had to call the ...(?). . . out in the back with the police there, and you could just go across the field anywhere. They didn't get on the road; just get in the car, tear out right across the field and come out on a road way over (?) somewhere.

So one of them cowboys said, "That nigger's blowin' that horn up there that's got a crooked neck to it, so I'm gonna see...I must kill." Shot up at it. Shot right at it, but it didn't hit nobody. Shot right around the neck of that horn of
Buster Smith - 63
that boy playing saxophone. So the boys were slippin' out one by one...
Did he actually hit the saxophone?
No. He missed it.
He missed it.
Yeah.
And missed the guy, too.

Uh-huh. So one of the cowboys was talking, and he said, "Man, you're gonna stop the band from playing. We've got to dance with these women here. You don't want to stop the band from playing. Don't do that." So he didn't shoot any more. But anyway, the band, when it got to about quittin' time, when that band was about to take an intermission, they said, "Oh, we got to get out of here some way or another. Someone go out there and get the car started." First man who got out was the drummer. See, them cowboys got kind of half-drunk and dancing with their women, they wasn't paying no attention. There was about 12 of them, 12 or 13, and they went out one by one. And it got clean on down to the piano player. He was the last man playing, sitting up on the bandstand. And them cowboys wasn't lookin'; they was still dancing. He didn't have to (?) . He just jumped up and grabbed his hat and put it on his head and ran out the door, and jumped in the car, and they was gone. The cowboys, they looked around, and the band's gone. "Where's the band at?!"
Buster Smith - 64
They was half-a-mile down the road, across the field.
When that had happened, of course, that meant the guys didn't get paid.

No. The boss ended up paying them. He knew something like that was liable to happen. That wasn't nothin' new to him. That had been going on with other bands. So he just paid them off, paid the boys, and he's going home. Heh-heh.
You know Snub Mosely?
Snub Mosely? Yeah.

He told me a story about some band -- this was right in the early 20's, I think, maybe '25. He said there was a band (I can't remember), the Golden Something, out of Chicago or somewhere. They were down in Florida, and somebody accused one of the band of stepping out of line or peeking at his woman or something.
Yeah, uh-huh.
And they waited for those guys after the gig, and they castrated a lot of them. That's what he told me.
Yeah. I knew Snub. He was in the last band I played with, up in New York. Cab was down there in St. Petersburg, and we had a drummer down there with us in Don Redman's band that had got hit.
Got hit?
Yeah.
Buster Smith - 65
How do you mean?

A guy throws a Coca-Cola bottle at Cab and missed him, and hit the drummer. And the drummer then left Cab and went with us, in Don Redman's band. He said, "I hope it don't happen tonight what happened then." And some of the boys say, "What happened?" He said, "A guy threw a bottle at Cab Calloway and missed him, and hit me." Cab thought he was White. You know, he's light... He thought he was White, and he was talking to some White woman. A fellow asked him to play some number, and he was talking to her, and he said, "We'll try to get to it," and this guy thought that he was flirting with some of the women, and he grabbed a Coca-Cola bottle and threw at Cab and missed him, and hit the drummer.
[PAUSE]
One of the other guys, I think it was Buddy Tate, was telling me that at some of the dances, where you'd have some White and some Black, they'd put a rope down the middle.
Yeah, yeah.
Is that what they used to do?
Yeah.
Would that have been in just the small places?
No, the big places.
The big places, too.
We had one here, at the (?) Hall. When I played
Buster Smith - 66
out there, we had three bands there, and they had a rope right down the middle...
And you had White one side and Black the other.
And White on one side. And they broke that up.
What happened?
Lloyd Jefferson was playing from 3 until...
Lloyd...?
Lloyd Jefferson. Little band. He was playing from I think 3 to 8. I was playing from 8 to 12, and then Calhoun from 12 to 4 in the morning.
These were three Black bands?

Yeah. Three Black bands. And we was the populest (sic) band that was in town. Later on, I found that the lady that was running the other club where we had been playing didn't have no band up... She had a band up there to play for her, and the band was going out there working at this place. So she got in... Anyway, she sent the lawyers out there. The sheriff come out there, him and another man, and he said he was a lawyer, and then one of the men that killed Clyde Barrow in that big dusty raid(?) we had down here back then. Tall guy who carried a long rifle, a 30-30. He was with him. Them three came out there and stopped the dance, run all the people out of the hall.
Was that because they didn't like Black and White dancers in the same room?
Buster Smith - 67

Yeah. So I was staying out there, because my car had broke down and the man who was working on it had taken three or four days to get it fixed -- and I was staying out there with one of the bosses. Another thing, the two bosses -- one of them was colored, one was White. But the colored was staying upstairs in the (?) Hall. He had an apartment up there. It was a big place called the Coconut Grove.
Here in Dallas.

Yeah. Right here in West Dallas. So I happened to be sitting there by the phone at the front door, the next day about 3 o'clock. And one of them sheriffs called down there from the County Jail, and says, "Is Taylor there?" -- that's the White man. I said "No." I answered the phone. I said, "No." There was a boy in there cleaning-up, sweeping going on back there. So I said, "No." He said, "Well, who are you?" I said, "Well, I'm one of the bandleaders. I'm Buster Smith." So he says, "Is Taylor there?" I said, "No, he's not here." "Well, is Fagin(?) there?" -- that's the colored boss. I said, "He's not here either. He's gone." He said, "Well, I'm one of the lawyers out there last night." He said, "You tell them don't let them White folks back in there no more. If you let them in, they're liable to start a riot. We don't want that." He said, "Don't let them in there, and there won't be no more trouble. There won't be no more raidin' out there." I said, "All right, officer. I'll tell
Buster Smith - 68
them." He said, "You'll tell them?!" "I sure will."

So soon they got back, and they had ten policemen hired there to keep order. He got two brothers out there called the Foreman(?) Brothers. Said, "They can fire any of them policemen they want, but they can't fire no Foreman(?) Brothers. They got to keep them Foreman(?) Brothers there. They got to keep them there. That's what I tell ...(?)."

When they came... They got there a little before the early band started, the first band, and I told them about it. So the first thing the colored manager said was, "Oh, they can't tell us... We paid them policemen out of our pocket. Paid them ourselves. They can't tell us who to fire and who to keep." I said, "Well, I can tell you what the man said. He said if we keep the White folks out of here we're all right." That happened on the Saturday night. We had to let it run all week until the next Saturday; they wouldn't let the White folks back no more. But the next Saturday night, there wasn't nothin' there but colored folks. They waited until I stopped playing, and Red had been playing for about an hour to come in there and raid the place anyhow. Run all the colored people, they throwed all the whiskey out all over...
Even though there were no White people there.
There were no White people nowhere around. The Texas Rangers had come up there that time.
Buster Smith - 69
What date was this? When did this happen?
In '48. '48 or '49, somewhere along there.
I see. Later on.
Yeah.
Do you think things got worse in that respect? I mean, in the early 40's were things easier from a racial point of view?
That was '47. That's when it was. '47 or '46.
Right. But I found out what it was. It was the lady running the other place...
She was fed up because she hadn't got a band.
Yeah. She didn't have no band, because we was drawing all the people out with our three bands playing out there. She had a little old band playing the place where she was...
[PAUSE]
...raised another point, about the size of bands. Now, going back to 1932, '33, '34, you get these little bands going around, these territory bands, like the Blue Devils.
Yes.
What was the average size of the bands? How many people roughly would you find in a band like that? Because it wasn't as big as 16 or 17 pieces...
Oh, no. Five and six pieces.
Five and six? As small as that.
Buster Smith - 70
Yes. And three. Sometimes you'd find three. And two! It was small. It wouldn't be no big house.
So in fact, the Blue Devils was rather bigger than usual.
Oh yeah. Yeah.
It was a bigger band than usual.
We had 13. And Trent had 12 or 13.
Did you know Eli Rice?
Yeah.
How many pieces would he carry?
I think he had around about 11 or 12.
That's quite a big band, too.
Uh-huh, yeah.
So who were the smaller bands? Can you think of any names? Eddie and Sugar Lou, I suppose, was one.
Yeah, Eddie and Sugar Lou had a small band. Let me see who else...
What about Coy's Black Aces?

No, they had a pretty big band. And Red Calhoun started out for a little while, I think, had a little small band. But mostly all the bands... And, like, uh... What was the name of the big band that went up to Omaha... Big fat boy who played...
Lateau(?).
Lateau(?). His band was a big band.
Yeah. Most of the bands back then were large bands.
Buster Smith - 71
The Carolina Cotton Pickers....
Yeah, all of those.
And Clarence Love.
Clarence Love...
They were all 10- and 12-piece.
Yeah.
All of them had 12 and 15 pieces. Up to 16.
And of course, there were a lot of small bands going around.
Yeah...
Ray Cooper had...
He had five or six pieces, like that, a little band...
It would be what? One trumpet, one trombone, one saxophone and a rhythm section?
Yeah.
Would most of the bands carry a vocalist? A singer.
Yeah.
Would it be a man or a woman?
A woman. Mostly in them days it was women.
Really.
Yeah.
Would they just sing ballads, or would they sing the jump tunes, too?
They'd sing anything. Everything.
Buster Smith - 72
Would there be young girls or would they be like older women?
Mostly seasoned women. They wouldn't carry no young girls, though. You'd run into some of them a lot of times, them young girls. They mostly had older women.
Yes, I see. Someone like Jimmy Rushing, then, was unusual? You wouldn't normally carry a blues singer with a band like that?
Yeah, Jimmy Rushing sang all of it. Everything. And Pha Terrell with Clouds of Joy, he sang everything. Yeah. Most all of them sing all of it. They wouldn't hire them if you couldn't sing everything.
What I mean is, it was more common to have a woman than a man.
Yeah.
A man was less usual.
Uh-huh. A woman, they figured that would draw the crowd.
A bit of glamour.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Dress her up in a pretty dress.
Yeah, dress her up and have her on the placard. They're still doing that now.
Oh sure.
I used to go to Oklahoma all the time, and I'd
Buster Smith - 73
carry a girl with me all the time. One time I had two boy singers, but I had a show along with it, and they had a bunch of girls in the show.
Oh, like a little dancing act?
Uh-huh. Dancing. Chorus girls and whatnot.
Was that before the War or after?
No, after the War.

Coming on to Bennie Moten and those days. Now, as I remember... Well, no, I don't remember. Just tell me, how did it happen that the Blue Devils managed to get to record? Because they just made those two or three sides, didn't they.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Which I don't think I've ever heard, incidentally. But how did that recording come about, and why did you not make more recordings?

Well, I don't know whether they couldn't catch up with us or we couldn't get together on nothin'. It just happened one man came through Oklahoma City, and he recorded us. Then so many guys came around through and tell you they're going to do some recording, and then we find out we wasn't going to get no money and the band wouldn't play. That's what the main thing was. In them days, most of what we'd heard of was Decca and two or three other companies. But these guys, they couldn't show us no credentials where they was from these recording companies. So
Buster Smith - 74
we wouldn't take no chances on them. Or we took money to do so record, and they're still doing that today, and we get no pay.
So in other words, what you're saying is that you got offers to record.
Yeah.
But you'd turn them down.

Yeah. There was too much fraud in it. And they want you to record originals two and two. Some of those originals have never been heard. Somebody made it up in the band, or some arrangement or something else, some music composer or something. And that's where they had double money. They had two ways to hit. I made several records where I didn't get nothin' out of it. Guys taking it and putting the things out down here in Louisiana and some of it out in West Texas, but it never did show up here in Dallas. And I just happened to be going through Wichita Falls, and we stopped there one night on the way going up to Amarillo or somewhere out there. But anyway, we stopped there and was eating dinner, and I went over to the jukebox to look, and there's my record sitting up there on the jukebox. And the man, the last time I'd seen him... I hadn't seen him in nearly a year, and he told me the record didn't do no good; it didn't even come out. Then I found out he was down in Mississippi, down there putting them out.
[PAUSE]
Buster Smith - 75
It's just a great pity that the recordings that the Blue Devils did make, you didn't have the best people in the band.
No.
I mean, Basie had gone by then, and Page had gone... [IN JAZZ STYLES, RUSSELL SAYS BASIE WAS ON THE SESSION AND CITES BASIE]
No, Page was there when we made that "Blue Devil Blues."
Walter Page.

Walter Page. We had Hot Lips Page. Jimmy Rushing was there. But see, we didn't branch out nowhere. The furthest we went up was Kansas City. Se, we didn't get around to them recording stations. Not that we made any. We made "Blue Devil Blues" right there in Oklahoma City at a radio station. The man just set up a little outfit and (?), and I think we had to pay money to do that.
Did the Blue Devils ever do any radio work?
No.
Never broadcast.
No. Damn shame.
And as far as you know, no one ever came along to any of the Blue Devils' gigs, like an amateur with a recording machine, and made any recordings at all.
No.
Buster Smith - 76
No one in the band ever made any recordings.
No.
Not even amateur ones, private ones.
No. I don't remember it. Uh-huh. Not a one.
What happened when the Blue Devils finally broke up? Why did the band break up in the end?
Well, after Walter Page left, Jimmy Rushing was gone because he wasn't no leader -- he wouldn't lead nothin'... But anyway, then Hot Lips left; he didn't want to be no leader.
Did they all leave to go to Moten?
Yeah. Every one of them. One by one.
Even Hot Lips.
Yeah.
And was this because Moten was saying to the guys, "You come with me; I'll give you more money"?

Yeah. He tried to get me first. But I didn't want to leave the Blue Devils. Because they didn't have no arranger, nobody to help them, and I didn't want to leave the boys, I liked the boys, and after they got Lester Young in there and Eight-Ball and all the boys, and Reuben Lynch and all them boys... I didn't want to leave 'em. Wouldn't leave 'em. I just stayed right along with 'em. Just went on. We just kept banging on (?). And it's a commonwealth band anyhow. I didn't know that a commonwealth band wasn't going to (?)be there(?).
Buster Smith - 77
What broke up the band... I'll get to that. We went back to Virginia the second time.
Is this West Virginia or Virginia?
Old Virginia. And we got down there, around Newport News, and got stranded and couldn't get out.
What happens when you get stranded?
Well, we got down there during the winter-time. You see most of the dates only was Catholic people...
Really?

Yeah. Especially the White folks. And we got down there, and the Catholic people ain't gonna go by the base until after Easter. So we got over there and got stranded over there, in Newport News, stayed over there, oh, about four or five months.
When you say you got stranded, you mean that you just didn't have the money to leave.
Yeah. We didn't have no car; the car was gone.
Instruments?

No, we had instruments. The car was gone. And we didn't have no money to leave, and couldn't pay nobody to take us nowhere because we wasn't workin' nowhere, couldn't get no gig nowhere, didn't have no car to go across...
How were you eating?
A man had a little old dance hall right on the
Buster Smith - 78
second floor down there, and we'd play there on the weekend for him, and he'd give us a little money...
It just gave you enough to eat for the week.
Yeah. From week to week.
And you could pay your board and lodging?

Yeah. Just enough money to pay our rent. Rent wasn't much. So we finally left there and came back to Martinsville, Virginia. We played a job up there. And we stayed up there. A colored doctor had a dance hall, and he let us play at his place Fridays and Saturdays. Just nothin' but a...
